bib.title: Lower Bounds: Basic Ideas (Chapter 13 of Bandit Algorithms)

question: How can a minimax lower bound on regret be motivated by reducing a bandit problem to two-hypothesis testing?
contributions: Defines worst-case and minimax regret and minimax optimality
States Theorem 13.1 (R*_n(E_k) >= c sqrt(kn)) with a heuristic two-instance proof; rigorous proof deferred to Chapter 15

results.claim: Minimax regret over k-armed unit-variance Gaussian bandits with means in [0,1] is at least c sqrt(kn) for a universal constant c (Theorem 13.1; proved in Ch. 15, only sketched here).
results.setup: E_k = k-armed Gaussian bandits, unit variance, means in [0,1]^k; all k>1 and n>=k; c universal and unspecified
results.note: Constant c is not given; the chapter only proves it heuristically.

results.claim: Heuristic bound: if E[T1(n)] < n/2 then regret under nu is at least (1/2) sqrt(n(k-1)); otherwise regret under nu' is about as large.
results.setup: nu has means (Delta,0,...,0); nu' differs only in arm i = argmin_{j>1} E[T_j(n)], set to 2 Delta; Delta = sqrt((k-1)/n) in (0,1/2]; assumes E[T1(n)] ~ E'[T1(n)] (not proven here)
results.quote: which completes our heuristic argument that there exists a universal constant
results.note: Heuristic: T_i(n) treated as non-random and indistinguishability of nu, nu' assumed.

results.claim: Under nu the least-played suboptimal arm satisfies E[T_i(n)] <= n/(k-1), which fixes Delta = sqrt(1/E[T_i(n)]) >= sqrt((k-1)/n).

Two-point Gaussian testing: with mu in {0,Delta}, unit variance, n samples, the midpoint test errs with probability about exp(-n Delta^2/8)/sqrt(n Delta^2); constant error if n is small relative to 8/Delta^2, exponentially small once n is large relative to 8/Delta^2.
results.setup: Known variance 1; error event mu-hat >= Delta/2 under mu=0; Eq. 13.1 bounds with constants 16 and 32/pi inside the square-root denominators
results.quote: then the procedure fails with constant probability.
results.note: Based on Gaussian tail bound Eq. 13.4 (Abramowitz and Stegun).

limits: Argument is heuristic: T_i(n) is random and the indistinguishability claim E[T1(n)] ~ E'[T1(n)] is not proven; needs information-theoretic tools (next chapter) and the proof in Ch. 15.
The chapter does not mention Bretagnolle-Huber, KL divergence, or any log n (instance-dependent) lower bound; it only motivates the sqrt(kn) minimax bound.
The universal constant c is never given.
Minimax optimality is a property of a policy, environment set and horizon; minimax policies may not exploit easy instances (note 2, Ch. 16).
practices: Select two instances that satisfy Competition (good action for one is bad for the other) and Similarity (policy cannot statistically identify which it faces); the bound comes from optimising this trade-off (p.181).
Build the alternative instance by raising the mean of the arm the policy expects to play least (p.182).
Prefer a nearly minimax policy with much lower regret on easy bandits over the exact minimax policy (note 2, p.183).

terms.definition: R_n(pi,E)=sup over nu in E of R_n(pi,nu)
R*_n(E)=inf over policies pi of sup over nu in E of R_n(pi,nu)
A policy with R_n(pi,E)=R*_n(E); a property of policy, environment set and horizon.
No other policy pi' has R_n(pi',nu)<=R_n(pi,nu) for all nu and strict inequality for at least one.

terms.term: minimax optimal up to constant factors
terms.definition: Exists C>0 with R_n(pi,E_k)/R*_n(E_k) <= C for all k and n.
